title: Naked Explanation
author: Pete Foster
summary: Pete Foster, writing primarily for new teachers, argues that PowerPoint slides which closely mirror a teacher's planned explanation quietly undermine the quality of that explanation, encouraging teachers to read or recite rather than genuinely explain, and making them less likely to check whether multi-step instructions were actually understood. He introduces "knowledge building is planning" as a diagnostic idea: some topics (he cites being able to explain Macbeth unprepared) a teacher can explain fluently without notice, while others genuinely require pre-lesson study, and reliance on slide bullet points often signals the latter kind of confidence gap rather than a neutral design choice. His practical suggestions split into background preparation - building topic knowledge deliberately, planning key phrases or story beats in advance, and building in a genuine understanding check - and foreground delivery tactics, including physically removing the PowerPoint as a competing stimulus by blanking the screen (the W or B keyboard shortcuts) and standing visibly in front of where it would be, so students' attention is redirected to the teacher's spoken words rather than the slide. He frames the whole exercise as naked explanation: deliberately explaining without the crutch of a mirrored slide, forcing the teacher's own knowledge and delivery to carry the lesson's cognitive weight, while stressing this is a matter of using PowerPoint more judiciously rather than abandoning it altogether.
points: Foster's diagnostic starting point is that PowerPoint slides mirroring what a teacher plans to say encourage reading or reciting rather than genuine explaining, and reduce the odds teachers check whether multi-step instructions actually landed.

His "knowledge building is planning" principle distinguishes topics a teacher can explain fluently unprepared from ones requiring genuine pre-lesson study, arguing slide reliance often masks a confidence gap rather than a design choice.

His foreground tactics get concrete about removing PowerPoint as a competing stimulus - blanking the screen mid-explanation and standing visibly in front of it - to physically redirect attention to the teacher's spoken explanation.

Foster frames the whole piece as naked explanation: deliberately stripping away slide-based scaffolding at the moment of explaining so that spoken language, not the screen, carries the cognitive weight of the lesson.
quotes: PowerPoint slides often mirror (sometimes exactly) what the teacher is going to say (about a topic or task with several steps) so the teacher either reads or recites the slide.
If complex tasks or topics are broken into steps on the PP slide, the teacher is less likely to check students have heard or understand instructions.

If you put me in front of a GCSE class studying Macbeth, I could explain various moments and concepts without needing time to plan. The same could not be said for Romeo and Juliet or The Merchant of Venice.
Weaving knowledge building into that planning process can make up for that lack of confidence.
Remove screen distractors. You can turn off your screen if it doesn’t take an age to come back on. Or, if in PowerPoint, you can press W or B to get a blank screen.

Stand visibly. If the screen if off, it could be directly in front of it. Practically we need to be able to see the whole class but just as important is communicating, perhaps implicitly, that what we’re saying is the most important thing to pay attention to right now.
At times, explanation works best as the sole vehicle for communicating knowledge.
